rich_text.plain_text: Astrup Fearnley Museet sits right on the water at Strandpromenaden 2, out at the end of Tjuvholmen on Oslo's central waterfront. The museum was founded in 1993 and later moved out here into a Renzo Piano building, or rather buildings: low volumes clad in timber the weather has taken to a soft silver-grey, under one long curved glass roof that steps straight over the canal running between them, carried on slender steel columns rigged like the masts in the harbour behind. Piano designed the park as well as the buildings. Behind it all sits a collection of nearly 1,500 works of international contemporary art, Jeff Koons, Damien Hirst, Cindy Sherman, Wolfgang Tillmans and Félix González-Torres among them, and the museum rehangs it rather than leaving it be.

rich_text.plain_text: , 12 June to 11 October 2026, more than 150 works spanning the Colombian painter's practice from the 1960s onwards. González died in January 2026, aged 93, so what was planned as a survey now reads as a memorial. She worked from images everyone had already seen, press photographs and famous European paintings, and repainted them flat and loud, in a palette that won't let you look past it. Not a difficult show to enjoy, and not an easy one to shake off. It's co-produced with the Pinacoteca de São Paulo and the Barbican in London, and curated here by the museum's director, Solveig Øvstebø.
